extracted.intended_audience: copyright policymakers, legal practitioners, stakeholders in copyright and AI (rights holders, AI developers, academics)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and policy criteria for determining when works involving AI are eligible for copyright protection, including whether human authorship or significant human input exists, alternative sui generis rights, and international approaches. Intended to guide registration, litigation, and legislative/policy decisions about AI-created content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human authorship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright requires human authorship; only a natural person can be considered an author and purely AI-generated works cannot be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most commenters and the Office view the Copyright Clause as requiring human authorship. The Office repeatedly states that because copyright requires human authorship, copyright law cannot be the basis of protection for works that do not satisfy that requirement. See related international responses noting that only natural persons can be authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant human input test
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated content may be eligible for copyright only if the human input in the creative process was significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The European Union member states shared the view that AI-generated content may be eligible 'only if the human input in [the] creative process was significant.' This functions as a threshold standard—mere minimal prompting may be insufficient; human contribution must meaningfully shape the final expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of authorship via prompts and subsequent modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A user's selection of multiple prompts and later adjustments/modifications can demonstrate the work is the result of the user's 'intellectual achievements' and personalized expression, supporting authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A Chinese court found that selection of over 150 prompts combined with subsequent adjustments showed the image resulted from the author's intellectual achievements, and thus the person who used AI was the author. Such factual indicia (number/quality of prompts, iterative human editing) are relevant evidence in registration/ litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory attribution for computer-generated works (UK-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a statute addresses computer-generated works, it may designate as 'author' the person 'by whom the arrangements necessary for the creation of the work are undertaken.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UK Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 contains such a provision and provides protection for computer-generated works (50-year term). Several commonwealth jurisdictions have similar statutory language (Hong Kong, India, New Zealand). The existence of such statutes affects ownership attribution when no human author is apparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between AI as assistive tool and as generator
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection is available when AI functions as a tool to assist human expression (assistive use), but not where AI independently generates expression without human authorship (generative use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office examples: registration of a sound recording created using a special-purpose AI vocal model as a tool for a human creative team (Randy Travis example). The Office stresses that when AI is used to recast, transform, or adapt an author's expression (assistive), the result can be protected; purely generative output lacking human authorship is not eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives justification for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: One argument for protecting AI-generated material is that legal protection would encourage creation of more works and further cultural and knowledge progress—i.e., copyright incentives promote production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents contend the Copyright Clause should be read flexibly to encompass new technologies and evolve to continue fostering innovation and artistic expression. Some commenters argued sui generis or amended copyright provisions could deliver these incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counter-incentives and policy harms test
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy analysis should weigh whether granting protection to AI outputs is necessary or could undermine the constitutional goal of incentivizing human authorship; AI systems do not need incentives and existing incentives to developers may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters argued AIs don't need incentives and that developers already receive incentives (patents, trade secrets, funding). The Office found the case for additional protection unpersuasive because of potential harms and existing incentives for AI developers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market dilution / content oversupply risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the risk that legal protection for AI-generated works would encourage proliferation of low-quality, high-volume AI outputs that dilute markets and reduce compensation for human creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/citations: UMG reported 'content oversupply' from an estimated 170 million AI-generated music tracks threatening royalties; Mechanical Licensing Collective royalty dilution; concerns that human creators will be crowded out or that copyright incentives will cease to function if markets are flooded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sui generis rights as alternative remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of creating specialized (sui generis) rights tailored to AI-generated works—defining eligibility, ownership, term, remedies differently from copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters proposed sui generis protection to address unique aspects like human input balance, term, and rightsholder identity. Most commenters opposed sui generis rights, citing similar concerns to copyright and problematic historical experience with such regimes (e.g., obsolescence, uncertainty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empowerment of creators with disabilities (assistive-use consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that extending protection when AI is used assistively can empower individuals with disabilities to create; protection should apply where AI acts as a tool enabling human expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters provided examples of assistive AI functionalities (text-to-speech, generative visual aids) enabling creators with disabilities. The Office supports empowering creators but emphasizes the legal distinction: protection is available for assistive uses where human authorship is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: International comparative approach / monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy and legal determinations should account for divergent international approaches and ongoing developments in other jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office notes varied approaches—EU member-state consensus leaning toward human input requirement, China's case law and draft proposals, UK statute for computer-generated works, Czechia case, Canada/Australia consultations—and states it is monitoring developments abroad to evaluate overlap or divergence with U.S. approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical and technological considerations (training data and quality effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how AI training practices (e.g., training on synthetic/AI-generated data) and technological dynamics affect the quality of outputs and the policy calculus for protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited research indicates 'degenerative AI' risks when systems train on their own outputs; synthetic data can lead to lower-quality results. These empirical factors inform whether legal protection would promote desirable creative outcomes or degrade them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership language and statutory definitions for computer-generated works
rubrics_metrics.description: When statutes define 'author' for computer-generated works (e.g., 'person who causes the work to be created' or 'person by whom the arrangements necessary for the creation of the work are undertaken'), those definitions determine who is treated as rightsholder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory examples: India §2(d)(vi) ('person who causes the work to be created'), Hong Kong and New Zealand provisions, and the UK’s formulation. The practical effect and interpretation of these phrases bear on registration and rights allocation where human authorship is ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy balancing: need for new incentives vs. potential to undermine human authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about extending protection should balance the argument that protection could drive creation and competition against evidence it may undermine incentives for human authors and the goals of the copyright system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office concluded it was not persuaded that additional protection is necessary, noting existing incentives for developers and potential harms—e.g., market crowding, reduced ability for human creators to earn livelihoods, and possible erosion of the quality and discoverability of inspiring works.
